photos.family_caption: Ellie and George, July 12 1968. Burlington City Hall steps.

raw_text_found: Handwritten on reverse in blue ink: 'Ellie & George — July 12, 1968 — our day'
Handwritten below in different (lighter) hand, added later: 'Burlington. The sun came out at noon.'
vision_extraction.scene_description: A young couple on stone steps in bright summer light. The woman — early 20s, dark hair pinned up with small white flowers — wears a simple A-line dress in cream with a lace overlay at the collar. She is laughing at something off-camera, not posed. The man — tall, glasses, a dark suit with a narrow tie — is looking at her with an expression of such undisguised delight that the photo feels almost private. White flowers in her hair. Behind them: the stone columns of what appears to be a civic building.
clothing_and_objects_noted: White flowers in Eleanor's hair (not a formal veil — small, informal, tucked in)
George's narrow-lapel dark suit — typical early 1960s cut, worn for a second or third time based on subtle wear at cuffs
No visible wedding rings yet in this shot — taken before the ceremony or immediately after
vision_extraction.emotional_register: Joy, slightly disbelieving. She is laughing; he is watching her laugh. This is a document of a person being seen.
personhood_map_additions: Wedding date confirmed: July 12, 1968
Location confirmed: Burlington, Vermont (City Hall steps)
Physical description of young Eleanor: dark hair, lace collar, informal white flowers — not a formal church wedding
George's character note: 'watching her laugh' — consistent with family description of patient devotion

The garden is productive and clearly loved but not fussed over.

photos.family_caption: Lemon drizzle day! Me and mom. I measured everything wrong and she didn't say a word. — Carol

raw_text_found: On the handwritten recipe card propped against the backsplash, partially legible: 'Lemon Drizzle — Ruth P. / ...flour, butter, sugar, 3 eggs... / FOR THE DRIZZLE: juice of 2 lemons + [illegible] sugar / Pour over while still warm — DO NOT WIPE'
At bottom of card in different handwriting (Eleanor's, identified by library desk photo comparison): 'Trust the drizzle. — E.M.'
On a small index card near the mixing bowl, in the same hand: 'Carol — the lemon goes in twice. Once in the batter. Once in the drizzle. Don't panic.'
On a blue ceramic mug on the counter: no text, but the chip on the rim is visible — this is Eleanor's mug
vision_extraction.scene_description: A bright kitchen. Two women — Eleanor (mid-70s) and Carol (early 50s) — stand at a butcher-block counter. Eleanor is pouring the lemon drizzle syrup from a small saucepan over the warm cake. Carol is watching with an expression that suggests she is resisting the urge to intervene. The recipe card is propped against the tile backsplash. The kitchen has the slightly worn warmth of a room used daily for decades — the spice rack, the old stand mixer, the blue mug.
clothing_and_objects_noted: Recipe card in Ruth's pencil handwriting — partially legible but the instruction 'Pour over while still warm — DO NOT WIPE' is clear
Eleanor's annotation at bottom: 'Trust the drizzle. — E.M.' — she wrote it on the card itself
Index card for Carol with instructions: 'Don't panic' — she prepared for Carol's anxiety

The old KitchenAid stand mixer at rear: 1970s model, avocado green
vision_extraction.emotional_register: Warm, conspiratorial. Eleanor is calm; Carol is hovering. The kitchen is doing what it has always done.
personhood_map_additions: Recipe card provenance confirmed: Ruth's pencil, Eleanor's ink addition ('Trust the drizzle. — E.M.')

photos.family_caption: The annual foliage drive. Stowe road, October 2012. Dad pulled over for every single tree.

raw_text_found: Handwritten on reverse: 'Stowe road, October 14 2012. G pulled over 11 times. Worth it.'
Partial sign visible at right edge of frame: 'BISHOP'S ORCHARD — APPLES CIDER'
On the car windshield interior (reflected in glass): a small laminated photo hanging from the mirror, too small to read
vision_extraction.scene_description: A two-lane rural road in peak Vermont autumn color. Maples line both sides — several are in the aggressive scarlet of peak color, a few still hold gold. In the foreground, one maple tree in particular dominates the left side of the frame, visibly more intensely red than its neighbors. A dark green car is pulled to the side of the road. A man (George, late 60s) stands in front of it looking up at the trees with his hands in his jacket pockets. A woman (Eleanor) is partially visible inside the car, window down, her arm resting on the door.
clothing_and_objects_noted: George's posture: hands in pockets, chin up, completely still — matching Ellie's description of him 'just standing there looking'
The one maple that is redder than the others — the one Eleanor described in her poem ('the outrageous red of being')
The farm stand sign at right: 'BISHOP'S ORCHARD — APPLES CIDER' — this is where they stop every year
Eleanor's arm on the door frame — she is watching him, not the trees
vision_extraction.emotional_register: Quiet, complete. Two people who have done this every October for decades. George is looking at the trees. Ellie is looking at George.
personhood_map_additions: The farm stand name confirmed: Bishop's Orchard (Stowe area) — specific detail for grounding conversations about the foliage drives
The 'one maple that turns first' is documented photographically — it is real, it is exactly as Ellie described it
George's habit of pulling over confirmed (note on reverse: 'G pulled over 11 times. Worth it.')
Ellie watching George, not the trees — the detail in the poem ('you lean into it') is about him as much as the maple
October 14, 2012 — 50 years after they met, approximately the 44th annual foliage drive
